blocks.text:
Lean's notation is built for a type checker, not for a reader. PLAER prints Lean as a mathematician would write it, using five rules. Each rule looks only at the *shape* of an expression and at its types, never at a particular name. To show this, every rule below is applied to Mathlib's own notions and to notions this paper defines itself, which no rule has ever heard of.

The claims here have no proofs attached; they are here for how they read. Switch any box to **Lean** to see what was written.

## 1. Assumptions about a type are hypotheses

In Lean, `[Group G]` asks Lean to find a group structure on $G$. It is an assumption, so it reads as one, in the same list as the other hypotheses. Every class prints as its own name.

/-- In a finite group, every element to the group's order is 1 -/
def Rules.pow_card : Prop :=
  ∀ (G : Type) [Group G] [Fintype G] (g : G), g ^ Fintype.card G = 1

/-- The smaller of two elements is at most either -/
def Rules.min_le : Prop := ∀ (α : Type) [LinearOrder α] (a b : α), min a b ≤ a

blocks.text: The same rule, for a class this paper defines:

/-- Something with a size -/
class Rules.Sized (α : Type) where
  size : α → ℕ

/-- Two equal things have the same size -/
def Rules.size_eq : Prop :=
  ∀ (α : Type) [Rules.Sized α] (a b : α), a = b → Rules.Sized.size a = Rules.Sized.size b

blocks.text:
## 2. Lean's encodings read as what they encode

Lean builds familiar objects out of functions and types. When an encoding is exactly a standard object, it prints as that object.

**Several inputs.** Lean's `ℝ → ℝ → ℝ` takes one input and returns a function. A mathematician writes a function of two inputs:

/-- A commutative operation on the reals -/
def Rules.commutative : Prop := ∀ f : ℝ → ℝ → ℝ, (∀ x y, f x y = f y x) → f 1 2 = f 2 1

items.doc: A commutative operation on the reals
items.name: Rules.commutative
items.statementLatex: \forall f : (\mathbb{R}, \mathbb{R}) \to \mathbb{R},\ (\forall x, y \in \mathbb{R},\ f(x, y) = f(y, x)) \implies f(1, 2) = f(2, 1)
items.statementLean: def Rules.commutative : Prop := ∀ (f : ℝ → ℝ → ℝ), (∀ (x y : ℝ), f x y = f y x) → f 1 2 = f 2 1
items.title: A commutative operation on the reals
items.source:
/-- A commutative operation on the reals -/
def Rules.commutative : Prop := ∀ f : ℝ → ℝ → ℝ, (∀ x y, f x y = f y x) → f 1 2 = f 2 1

blocks.text: **Functions given by a formula.** Lean writes `fun x => x ^ 2`; a mathematician writes $x \mapsto x^2$:

/-- Squaring is multiplying by itself -/
def Rules.square : Prop := (fun x : ℝ => x ^ 2) = (fun x => x * x)

blocks.text: **Sets used as types.** `Fin n` and `{x // p x}` are sets of numbers that Lean treats as types:

/-- Every element of Fin 5 is below 5 -/
def Rules.fin_lt : Prop := ∀ i : Fin 5, (i : ℕ) < 5

/-- A positive number is at least 1 -/
def Rules.positive : Prop := ∀ n : {n : ℕ // n > 0}, (n : ℕ) ≥ 1

blocks.text: **Values of a structure are tuples.** The same rule handles a structure this paper defines. A field that is a proof is never shown, so a `Digit`, a number with a proof that it is below 10, is just its number:

/-- A point in the plane, with integer coordinates -/
structure Rules.Point where
  x : ℤ
  y : ℤ

/-- The origin -/
def Rules.origin : Rules.Point := ⟨0, 0⟩

/-- A number below 10 -/
structure Rules.Digit where
  value : ℕ
  small : value < 10

/-- Seven, as a digit -/
def Rules.seven : Rules.Digit := ⟨7, by decide⟩

/-- Every digit is below 10 -/
def Rules.digit_lt : Prop := ∀ d : Rules.Digit, d.value < 10

blocks.text: **Limits.** Mathlib states limits with filters: `Tendsto f atTop (𝓝 a)`. That is $\lim_{x \to \infty} f(x) = a$:

items.doc: 1/n tends to 0
items.name: Rules.inverse_limit
items.statementLean: def Rules.inverse_limit : Prop := Filter.Tendsto (fun n => 1 / ↑n) Filter.atTop (nhds 0)
items.title: 1/n tends to 0
items.source:
/-- 1/n tends to 0 -/
def Rules.inverse_limit : Prop := Filter.Tendsto (fun n : ℕ => 1 / (n : ℝ)) Filter.atTop (nhds 0)

items.doc: Squares eventually pass 100
items.name: Rules.eventually_large
items.statementLean: def Rules.eventually_large : Prop := ∀ᶠ (n : ℕ) in Filter.atTop, n ^ 2 > 100
items.title: Squares eventually pass 100
items.source:

def Rules.eventually_large : Prop := ∀ᶠ n in Filter.atTop, n ^ 2 > (100 : ℕ)

blocks.text:
## 3. An unusual operation looks unusual

Some of Lean's operations differ from the textbook ones on ordinary inputs. They never print with the textbook symbol, and the box says what the symbol means.

/-- Subtracting and adding back can overshoot -/
def Rules.sub_add : Prop := ∀ n m : ℕ, n - m + m ≥ n

/-- Gauss's formula, with division in ℕ -/
def Rules.gauss_div : Prop := ∀ n : ℕ, ∑ i ∈ Finset.range (n + 1), i = n * (n + 1) / 2

/-- Division with remainder in ℤ -/
def Rules.div_mod : Prop := ∀ a b : ℤ, b * (a / b) + a % b = a

/-- Dividing a real number by itself -/
def Rules.div_self : Prop := ∀ x : ℝ, x ≠ 0 → x / x = 1

blocks.text:
## 4. A conversion shows only when it can change a value

$\mathbb{N} \subseteq \mathbb{Z} \subseteq \mathbb{Q} \subseteq \mathbb{R}$: a number moved into a larger number system is the same number, so the conversion prints as nothing. The test is general: a conversion is hidden exactly when it can never make two different numbers equal. For the conversions from $\mathbb{N}$, $\mathbb{Z}$ and $\mathbb{Q}$ that is when the target has characteristic zero. A conversion into $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ can make $1$ and $4$ equal, so it shows. In the first claim below, $n$ is moved into $\mathbb{R}$ twice; the conversions are invisible, and the two divisions still look different, because one is in $\mathbb{N}$ and one in $\mathbb{R}$.

/-- Half of n, in ℕ and in ℝ -/
def Rules.half : Prop := ∀ n : ℕ, ((n / 2 : ℕ) : ℝ) ≤ (n : ℝ) / 2

/-- Modulo 3, 1 and 4 are the same -/
def Rules.mod_three : Prop := ((1 : ℤ) : ZMod 3) = ((4 : ℤ) : ZMod 3)

/-- The floor of x is at most x -/
def Rules.floor_le : Prop := ∀ x : ℝ, (⌊x⌋ : ℝ) ≤ x

items.doc: Half of n, in ℕ and in ℝ
items.name: Rules.half
notes: $\lfloor a / b \rfloor$ is division in $\mathbb{N}$, rounded down; dividing by $0$ gives $0$.
items.statementLean: def Rules.half : Prop := ∀ (n : ℕ), ↑(n / 2) ≤ ↑n / 2
items.title: Half of n, in ℕ and in ℝ

blocks.text:
## 5. Elements are written as elements

A variable that ranges over the elements of a type reads $x \in T$, and one that ranges over subsets reads $S \subseteq T$. A variable that is itself a function, a type, or a proposition keeps $x : T$, because it is not an element of a set of numbers.

/-- Every real square is nonnegative -/
def Rules.sq_nonneg : Prop := ∀ x : ℝ, x ^ 2 ≥ 0

/-- Every set of naturals contains its own elements -/
def Rules.subset_refl : Prop := ∀ s : Set ℕ, s ⊆ s

/-- Every function has a value at 0 -/
def Rules.value_at_zero : Prop := ∀ f : ℕ → ℕ, ∃ n : ℕ, f 0 = n

/-- Every type's elements equal themselves -/
def Rules.refl : Prop := ∀ (α : Type) (x : α), x = x
